requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'CUDA-L2: Surpassing cuBLAS Performance for Matrix Multiplication through Reinforcement Learning' have been reproduced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware and software environment matches the paper: A100 GPU (Ampere), NVIDIA CUDA toolkit with nvcc, cuBLAS, cuBLASLt libraries, CUTLASS/CuTe, compute-sanitizer, and PyTorch for the torch.matmul baseline.
The GPU hardware environment matches the paper's A100 (Ampere) target platform.

Code has been implemented to detect and verify that the target GPU is an NVIDIA A100 (Ampere architecture, compute capability 8.0) before running benchmarks, aborting or warning if a different architecture is used.

verification.spec: Run the environment-check entrypoint on an A100 host and confirm it returns success/detects compute capability 8.0; run it (or simulate via mock) on a non-A100 device (e.g., different cudaDeviceProp.major/minor) and confirm it aborts or emits a warning. Inspect code for a query of cudaGetDeviceProperties (or torch.cuda.get_device_capability) and a branch that checks (major, minor) == (8, 0) or device name contains 'A100'.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to log the detected GPU device name, compute capability, driver version, and available memory at the start of every benchmark run so the hardware provenance of results is reproducible.

verification.spec: Invoke the benchmark entry point with a small (M,N,K) sample and capture stdout/stderr/log-file output. Assert the log contains a line reporting: GPU device name (matches `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name`), compute capability (e.g., '8.0' for A100), driver version, and total/available memory in MB or GB. Regex-match each field.

sub_tasks.requirements: The CUDA toolkit and compilation environment for building custom HGEMM .cu kernels is set up correctly.
Code has been implemented to invoke nvcc to compile generated HGEMM kernels from .cu source files with the -arch=sm_80 flag (or equivalent Ampere-targeting flag) required for A100 tensor core code.

verification.spec: Invoke the kernel build pipeline on a sample generated .cu file and capture the nvcc command line (e.g., by wrapping nvcc or inspecting build logs/Makefile/CMake). Assert the command contains '-arch=sm_80' or '-gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80'. Also confirm the resulting binary contains SASS for sm_80 via `cuobjdump --list-elf` or `cuobjdump -sass`.

sub_tasks.requirements: The build configuration links against cuBLAS and cuBLASLt (-lcublas -lcublasLt) and includes cublas_v2.h and cublasLt.h headers so that the baseline kernels described in Section 2.2 can be built and executed.

verification.spec: Grep the build files (Makefile / CMakeLists.txt / setup.py) for '-lcublas' and '-lcublasLt' link flags, and grep baseline source files for '#include <cublas_v2.h>' and '#include <cublasLt.h>'. Confirm the baseline binary links against libcublas.so and libcublasLt.so via `ldd`.

sub_tasks.requirements: The nvcc toolchain version used supports the CUTLASS/CuTe headers required by CUDA-L2 generated kernels (i.e., a CUDA toolkit version >= 12.0 with a matching CUTLASS release providing the CuTe library).

verification.spec: Run `nvcc --version` and assert release version >= 12.0. Verify a CUTLASS release providing CuTe is available by locating the header `cutlass/include/cute/tensor.hpp` on the include path. Compile a tiny .cu file that #include's <cute/tensor.hpp> and a simple cute::make_tensor call; assert nvcc returns exit code 0.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to make CUTLASS/CuTe header include paths available to nvcc when compiling generated kernels, so that kernels using cute:: abstractions (e.g., partition_fragment_A, tiled_mma, Copy_Atom<UniversalCopy<uint128_t>>) compile without errors.

verification.spec: Compile a small test .cu file that uses cute::partition_fragment_A, cute::TiledMMA, and Copy_Atom<UniversalCopy<cute::uint128_t>, half> via the project's kernel-compilation entry point (same nvcc invocation used for generated kernels). Assert exit code 0 and no missing-header errors in stderr.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to enforce a per-kernel compile-and-launch timeout so that runaway compilations or executions do not block the pipeline, consistent with the paper's requirement that a kernel executes to completion within a reasonable time limit.

verification.spec: Submit a kernel source that contains an infinite loop (e.g., `while(1);` inside the kernel) to the compile-and-launch pipeline. Assert the pipeline returns a timeout status within the configured limit (e.g., <120 seconds) rather than hanging indefinitely. Repeat for compile-time by submitting pathological template code and verify compile-timeout is enforced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The compute-sanitizer memcheck integration for checking kernel executability is available and wired into the evaluation pipeline.

Code has been implemented to invoke `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` on each compiled kernel binary and to parse its exit code / output to classify the kernel as executable vs. having memory access violations, as specified in Section 2.3.1.

verification.spec: Feed the executability checker two synthetic kernel binaries: (a) a correct kernel, (b) a kernel with a deliberate out-of-bounds write. Assert the checker invokes `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` (verify via process trace or logs), parses its output/exit code, and classifies (a) as executable and (b) as having memory access violations.

sub_tasks.requirements: The compute-sanitizer binary is available on the PATH used by the evaluation scripts (installed as part of the CUDA toolkit) and the pipeline fails fast with a clear error if it cannot be found.

verification.spec: Run `which compute-sanitizer` and assert exit code 0 and a non-empty absolute path. Then temporarily rename the binary (or prepend a PATH stub) and invoke the evaluation pipeline; assert it exits with a clear error message mentioning 'compute-sanitizer' rather than silently skipping the memcheck.

sub_tasks.requirements: The PyTorch environment used to run the torch.matmul baseline is installed and configured consistently with the paper.

A PyTorch build with CUDA support is installed such that `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns True and torch.matmul on FP16 tensors dispatches to the GPU cuBLAS backend, matching the setup described in Section 2.2.1.

verification.spec: Import torch and assert torch.cuda.is_available() is True. Create A=torch.randn(512,512,dtype=torch.float16,device='cuda'), B=torch.randn(512,512,dtype=torch.float16,device='cuda'), call torch.matmul(A,B), and assert the result is on cuda and dtype float16. Additionally profile with torch.profiler and assert a cuBLAS-family kernel (e.g., 'cutlass' or 'gemm') is executed on the GPU.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to construct FP16 (half-precision) input tensors on the CUDA device for the torch.matmul baseline, matching HGEMM's input dtype (torch.float16).

verification.spec: Invoke the torch.matmul baseline setup function for (M,N,K)=(256,256,256). Assert the returned A and B tensors satisfy: A.dtype==torch.float16, B.dtype==torch.float16, A.device.type=='cuda', B.device.type=='cuda', A.shape==(256,256), B.shape==(256,256).

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that uses torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) with torch.cuda.synchronize() before start and between end and elapsed_time to measure kernel execution time exactly as shown in Listing 1 of the paper.

verification.spec: Locate the kernel-timing function in the codebase and assert its source contains, in order: (1) torch.cuda.synchronize() before Event creation, (2) torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) for both start and end, (3) start_event.record() before kernel call, (4) end_event.record() after kernel call, (5) torch.cuda.synchronize() before elapsed_time, (6) start_event.elapsed_time(end_event) to return the ms. Use AST parsing or regex on the source file.

sub_tasks.requirements: GPU runtime environment controls (streams, clocks, memory) are configured to give stable measurements as described in Sections 2.4 and 4.1.

Code has been implemented to run all custom and baseline kernels on the default CUDA stream and to reject or flag generated kernels that create additional CUDA streams, matching the anti-timing-hacking rule stated in Section 2.4.1.

verification.spec: Submit a candidate .cu kernel that contains `cudaStreamCreate` to the kernel validator. Assert the validator rejects it with a message referencing 'stream'. Also verify baseline execution: run a valid kernel and confirm it executes on the default stream (stream 0) by profiling with nvprof/nsys and checking stream id.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to allocate a persistent cuBLASLt workspace buffer (used as the `workspace` / `ws_size` arguments in the cublasLtMatmul calls shown in Listings 7 and 8) and to reuse it across all benchmark iterations.

verification.spec: Instrument the cuBLASLt baseline initialization. Assert that a device buffer of size `ws_size` (>0, e.g., 32MB as commonly used) is cudaMalloc'd once at setup. Call the baseline evaluation twice for the same (M,N,K) and verify the same workspace pointer is reused (no additional cudaMalloc calls between invocations, checked via cuda-memcheck or a cudaMalloc hook).

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented to initialize a single global cuBLAS handle (`g_handle`) and a cuBLASLt matmul preference object (`pref`) once at startup and reuse them across all baseline calls, matching the API usage in Listings 6-8.

verification.spec: Search for the global cuBLAS handle (`g_handle`) and cuBLASLt preference (`pref`) initialization in the codebase. Assert cublasCreate and cublasLtMatmulPreferenceCreate are each called exactly once in the initialization path (grep + runtime hook to count invocations across a full benchmark run over 10 configurations).

sub_tasks.requirements: The 1,000 (M,N,K) configuration grid is enumerated, and kernel executability (compile, launch, memcheck) plus correctness criteria (exact-match with binary inputs, baseline-bounded deviation) are implemented as described in Section 2.3.
The full 1,000-configuration (M,N,K) grid is enumerated exactly as described.
Code has been implemented that defines the base dimension set {64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 12288, 16384} used to construct (M,N,K) triplets.

verification.spec: Import the configuration module and assert the base dimension list equals exactly [64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 12288, 16384] (as a sorted list/tuple). Additionally assert len==10 and that the Cartesian product produces 1000 (M,N,K) triplets.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that enumerates the full Cartesian product of the 10 M values, 10 N values and 10 K values, producing exactly 1,000 unique (M,N,K) configurations.

verification.spec: Call the configuration-generation function and collect its output. Assert len(configs) == 1000, that the set of M-values, N-values, and K-values each equals {64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192,12288,16384}, and that configs equals the Cartesian product of those three sets.

sub_tasks.requirements: The enumerated configuration grid contains exactly 1000 entries with no duplicates, verified programmatically before evaluation.

verification.spec: Load the enumerated configuration list used to drive evaluation and assert len(set(configs)) == 1000 and len(configs) == 1000 (no duplicates). Confirm this check is run before evaluation begins (either as an assertion in the eval script or a unit test).

sub_tasks.requirements: Kernel executability checks (compile, launch, run-to-completion, memcheck) are implemented.
Code has been implemented that compiles candidate HGEMM kernels from .cu source files using nvcc and reports a compilation-failure status when compilation fails.

verification.spec: Write a valid tiny HGEMM .cu file and submit it to the compilation entry point; assert exit status indicates success and the resulting .so/executable exists. Then submit a .cu file with a syntax error and assert the entry point returns a distinct compilation-failure status with nvcc stderr captured.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that launches the compiled kernel and enforces a reasonable time limit, marking the kernel as failed if it does not run to completion within the limit.

verification.spec: Compile a kernel that intentionally spins on the device (e.g., a while(clock64()<huge_value) loop). Submit it to the launch pipeline with a timeout (e.g., 60s) and assert the pipeline returns a 'timeout' or 'failed' status within timeout+small-margin seconds, and does NOT hang the test process.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that runs `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` on each candidate kernel and rejects kernels reporting memory access violations.

verification.spec: Submit a kernel that writes out of bounds (e.g., idx = threadIdx.x + 1e9) to the memcheck pipeline. Assert the pipeline invokes `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` (verified via strace or a wrapper) and rejects the kernel (returns failed status with sanitizer stderr in the log). Submit a clean kernel and assert it passes.

sub_tasks.requirements: A kernel is classified as 'successful' if and only if it compiles, launches, runs to completion within the time budget, and passes memcheck; the pipeline exposes this boolean status for downstream reward and evaluation.

verification.spec: Call the pipeline's `is_successful(kernel_source)` (or equivalent) API on: (a) a valid clean kernel — expect True; (b) a kernel with syntax error — expect False; (c) a kernel that times out — expect False; (d) a kernel with OOB memory access — expect False. Verify the boolean is returned/exposed through the public API used by the reward computation.

sub_tasks.requirements: The FP32 CPU reference implementation used for correctness checks is implemented.
Code has been implemented that computes C = A*B on CPU using FP32 arithmetic, given FP16/binary input matrices A (M x K) and B (K x N), and returns an FP32 reference output C_ref.

verification.spec: Call the FP32 CPU reference function with A=numpy.eye(4,dtype=float16) and B=numpy.eye(4,dtype=float16). Assert output dtype is float32 and equals np.eye(4,dtype=float32) exactly. Also call with random binary A (4x8) and B (8x4); assert output equals A.astype(float32)@B.astype(float32) exactly.

sub_tasks.requirements: The FP32 CPU reference produces bit-identical integer results when inputs are drawn from {0,1}, verified by a unit test on a small (M,N,K) instance.

verification.spec: Generate A (16x16) and B (16x16) with values sampled uniformly from {0,1} using a fixed seed. Call the FP32 CPU reference twice and assert both outputs are bit-identical (np.array_equal). Also assert every element equals the analytical integer sum computed via numpy int64 matmul.

sub_tasks.requirements: The exact-match correctness criterion using binary {0,1} inputs is implemented as described in Section 2.3.2.

Code has been implemented that randomly generates A and B matrices with elements drawn from {0,1}, with the binary probability adjustable based on matrix sizes so that a significant proportion of reference output entries fall in (0, 2048).

verification.spec: Call the binary-matrix generator for a set of (M,N,K) sizes covering small (128,128,128) and large (4096,4096,4096). Assert every element of A and B is in {0,1}. Compute the FP32 reference C=A@B and assert that at least 30% of the entries of C fall in (0, 2048). Verify the generator's probability parameter is a function of K (e.g., decreases with K).

sub_tasks.requirements: For each position (i,j) with C_ref[i,j] < 2048, the check requires C_custom[i,j] == C_ref[i,j] exactly; positions with C_ref[i,j] >= 2048 are ignored.

verification.spec: Feed the correctness checker synthetic C_ref and C_custom tensors: (a) all values <2048 and equal — must pass; (b) all values <2048 with a single differing entry — must fail; (c) entries with C_ref>=2048 differing between ref and custom while all <2048 entries match — must pass (large entries ignored). Assert behavior matches for each case.

sub_tasks.requirements: The exact-match test is repeated multiple times with independently sampled random binary inputs, and the kernel is marked incorrect if any single iteration fails.

verification.spec: Instrument the exact-match test to count iterations and to accept a mock kernel that fails on a specific iteration index. Assert (i) the number of iterations with fresh random binary A,B is > 1 (e.g., N_iters >= configured value), (ii) if any single iteration mismatches the kernel is classified incorrect (short-circuit or full-run — either acceptable). Verify inputs across iterations differ (RNG advanced).

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral test demonstrates the exact-match check flags a deliberately wrong kernel (e.g., off-by-one accumulation) as incorrect and accepts a correct reference-equivalent kernel.

verification.spec: Write two test kernels: (1) a correct HGEMM (e.g., simple triple-loop tensorcore or a wrapped cuBLAS call) — assert the exact-match checker returns True. (2) a deliberately wrong kernel that adds 1 to every output element — assert the checker returns False. Also assert the checker uses only reference entries where C_ref < 2048 (positions with C_ref >= 2048 ignored).

sub_tasks.requirements: The baseline-bounded deviation correctness criterion is implemented as described in Section 2.3.2.

Code has been implemented that runs the set of trusted NVIDIA baseline kernels (cuBLAS-NN, cuBLAS-TN, cuBLASLt-heuristic-NN, cuBLASLt-heuristic-TN, cuBLASLt-AutoTuning-NN, cuBLASLt-AutoTuning-TN) on the same test input and collects their outputs.

verification.spec: Import the module implementing the baseline runner. Verify it exposes a callable (e.g., run_baselines(A, B)) that invokes all six NVIDIA baseline kernels: cuBLAS-NN, cuBLAS-TN, cuBLASLt-heuristic-NN, cuBLASLt-heuristic-TN, cuBLASLt-AutoTuning-NN, cuBLASLt-AutoTuning-TN. Call it with a small (M,N,K)=(128,128,128) FP16 input pair and confirm it returns 6 output tensors, all shape (M,N), dtype float16, and pairwise close within FP16 tolerance.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that computes the maximum elementwise absolute difference among the trusted baseline kernel outputs and uses it as the deviation upper bound for that test input.

verification.spec: Provide a stub baseline set of 3+ known FP16 output tensors with a known pairwise max elementwise diff D. Call the deviation-bound computation and assert its returned bound equals max over all baseline pairs of ||O_i - O_j||_inf (equivalently max_i ||O_i - mean||_inf per paper wording — accept the max pairwise formulation). Verify the trusted baselines used are exactly {cuBLAS-NN, cuBLAS-TN, cuBLASLt-heuristic-NN, cuBLASLt-heuristic-TN, cuBLASLt-AutoTuning-NN, cuBLASLt-AutoTuning-TN}.

sub_tasks.requirements: A custom kernel is marked incorrect if its maximum elementwise absolute deviation from the FP32 CPU reference output exceeds the computed baseline-derived upper bound.

verification.spec: Given a fixed FP32 CPU reference C_ref and a baseline-derived deviation bound D, feed the checker two custom outputs: (a) max|C_custom - C_ref| = 0.5*D → must be classified correct; (b) max|C_custom - C_ref| = 2*D → must be classified incorrect. Assert both classifications.

sub_tasks.requirements: A behavioral test demonstrates that a kernel whose output deviation exceeds the baseline bound is rejected while a kernel whose output is within the bound is accepted.

verification.spec: Construct two synthetic 'custom' outputs: (a) one equal to cuBLAS-NN's output plus tiny noise below the max pairwise baseline diff; (b) one perturbed by 10x that baseline bound. Feed both through the correctness checker along with the six baseline outputs and FP32 reference. Assert (a) is accepted (returns True/correct) and (b) is rejected (returns False/incorrect).

sub_tasks.requirements: The overall kernel-successfulness pipeline combining executability and both correctness criteria is implemented.

Code has been implemented that a kernel is declared 'successful' only if it passes executability (compile+launch+memcheck), the exact-match binary-input test, and the baseline-bounded deviation test; failure in any stage marks the kernel as unsuccessful.

verification.spec: Invoke the kernel success checker on four synthetic kernels: (1) a kernel that fails to compile, (2) one that compiles but has an out-of-bounds memory access flagged by compute-sanitizer, (3) one that passes executability but returns wrong output on binary {0,1} inputs, (4) one that passes all three stages. Confirm only kernel (4) is reported successful and each of (1)-(3) is failed at the expected stage.

sub_tasks.requirements: The success/failure status is exposed per (M,N,K) configuration so downstream RL reward and speedup measurement only apply to successful kernels.

verification.spec: Run the evaluation pipeline on a small list of (M,N,K) configs including at least one that is known-good and one known-broken. Inspect the returned data structure (e.g., dict keyed by (M,N,K)) and confirm each entry has a boolean 'success' field; then verify that reward/speedup computation code branches on this field so unsuccessful entries are excluded from speedup aggregates.

sub_tasks.requirements: The benchmarking protocol is implemented: single-run speedup formula, 10s warmup + 30s minimum run, randomized ordering, offline and server modes (kernels at random intervals with intervals excluded from timing), and anti-hacking measures (no extra CUDA streams, .cu files).
Timing measurement primitives are implemented for HGEMM kernels using CUDA events with proper synchronization.

Code has been implemented that measures kernel execution time using torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) with start/end events, wrapping the kernel call between torch.cuda.synchronize() before start_event.record() and after end_event.record(), and computing elapsed_time_ms via start_event.elapsed_time(end_event), matching Listing 1.

verification.spec: Inspect the timing function source and assert the exact call sequence: torch.cuda.synchronize(); start_event = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True); end_event = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True); start_event.record(); <kernel call>; end_event.record(); torch.cuda.synchronize(); elapsed = start_event.elapsed_time(end_event). Verify via AST parse or regex-match against Listing 1.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that on each measurement iteration executes BOTH the custom kernel and the reference/baseline kernel, so a per-run pair (t_ref, t_custom) is available for the speedup formula.

verification.spec: Instrument the measurement loop with counters/mocks that record how many times custom_kernel and reference_kernel are invoked per iteration. Run for N=5 iterations and assert both counters equal 5 and that each iteration yields a (t_ref, t_custom) tuple with both values > 0.

sub_tasks.requirements: The single-run speedup is computed as s(custom) = t_ref / t_custom (i.e., ratio of reference execution time to custom execution time), as defined in Section 2.4.

verification.spec: Call the speedup computation with mocked t_ref=2.0 ms, t_custom=1.0 ms and assert returned value == 2.0. Try t_ref=1.0, t_custom=2.0 and assert returned value == 0.5. Confirm formula is t_ref / t_custom (not the inverse).

sub_tasks.requirements: Warmup and minimum-runtime policy for a single evaluation is implemented.
Code has been implemented that runs an untimed warmup phase of at least 10 seconds before any measured iteration begins.

verification.spec: Instrument the evaluation loop to record wall-clock time from loop start until the first measurement is recorded. Assert warmup phase >= 10.0 seconds. Also verify samples collected during warmup are discarded (not included in mean speedup).

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented that continues the measured evaluation loop until at least 30 seconds of measurement time have elapsed (minimum run length), and only then stops collecting samples.

verification.spec: Instrument the evaluation loop to record cumulative measurement time. Assert total measurement duration >= 30.0 seconds before termination. Verify the loop termination condition explicitly checks elapsed measurement time (not just iteration count).

sub_tasks.requirements: The final evaluation score for a (custom, reference) pair is computed as the mean of the per-run speedup scores s(custom) over all measured iterations, as specified in Section 2.4.

verification.spec: Monkey-patch the timers to return known synthetic (t_ref, t_custom) pairs across, e.g., 10 iterations. Compute expected mean of s = t_ref/t_custom analytically and confirm the evaluation function returns exactly that value (within 1e-6) as the final score.

sub_tasks.requirements: Randomized execution ordering is implemented to eliminate ordering effects.
Code has been implemented that, within each measured iteration, randomizes the execution order of the custom kernel and the reference kernel (rather than always calling them in a fixed order).

verification.spec: Wrap the custom and reference kernels with call-order-recording stubs. Run the measurement loop for 200 iterations with a fixed seed; count how many iterations invoked custom-before-reference vs reference-before-custom. Assert both counts are >0 and roughly balanced (each between 30% and 70%), confirming randomized ordering rather than fixed ordering.

sub_tasks.requirements: Offline and Server evaluation modes are implemented following the MLPerf-style protocol described in Section 2.4.2.
Code has been implemented for an Offline evaluation mode that executes kernels back-to-back with no inserted pauses/intervals between kernel launches.

verification.spec: Invoke the evaluator in offline mode with a dummy kernel that records wall-clock timestamps of each launch. Verify: (a) no explicit sleep/delay is inserted between consecutive kernel launches, and (b) the median inter-launch gap is <1ms (i.e., back-to-back). Contrast against server mode where the gap is significantly larger.

sub_tasks.requirements: Code has been implemented for a Server evaluation mode that inserts random idle intervals between consecutive kernel launches to simulate real-time inference request arrivals.

verification.spec: Run the server-mode evaluator with instrumentation that records timestamps of consecutive kernel launches. Assert that gaps between launches are non-zero and non-constant (drawn from a randomized distribution — e.g., std of gaps > 0). Compare against offline mode, where gaps should be near zero.

sub_tasks.requirements: In Server mode, the inserted idle interval time is explicitly excluded from the measured execution time used to compute the speedup ratio (only the actual kernel execution time contributes to t_ref and t_custom).

verification.spec: In server mode, inject a large sleep interval (e.g., 100 ms) between launches while running a kernel whose actual GPU time is ~1 ms. Assert the recorded t_custom used in the speedup is ~1 ms (kernel time only), not ~101 ms — i.e., the idle interval is excluded from the timed region between start_event/end_event.

sub_tasks.requirements: Both Offline and Server modes reuse the same warmup (10s), minimum runtime (30s), randomized ordering, and mean-speedup aggregation policy so that only the inter-kernel interval behavior differs between modes.

verification.spec: Inspect the offline and server evaluation entry points (source-level or via config introspection). Verify both use the same warmup duration (10s), same minimum measurement duration (30s), the same randomized-order flag, and the same mean aggregation; only the inter-launch interval configuration differs between them.

sub_tasks.requirements: Server-mode measurements exhibit larger per-configuration variance than Offline-mode measurements (consistent with the paper's observation that server mode allows the GPU to cool between requests, inducing clock-boost / throttling variability).

verification.spec: For a fixed (M,N,K) configuration (e.g., 2048,2048,2048), run the evaluator 5 independent times in offline mode and 5 times in server mode, collecting the per-run speedup values. Compute standard deviation across the 5 runs for each mode. Assert std(server) > std(offline).

sub_tasks.requirements: Anti-hacking measures for timing measurement are enforced, as described in Section 2.4.1.

Code has been implemented that rejects or fails compilation/evaluation of any candidate kernel that creates additional CUDA streams (e.g., cudaStreamCreate or torch.cuda.Stream) beyond the default stream, so that asynchronous stream tricks cannot be used to hide work outside the timed region.

verification.spec: Submit two candidate .cu/.py sources to the validation gate: (a) baseline kernel using only the default stream — must be accepted; (b) kernel that calls cudaStreamCreate/cudaStreamCreateWithFlags or torch.cuda.Stream() — must be rejected. Verify rejection message references stream creation.

sub_tasks.requirements: Candidate HGEMM kernels are emitted as CUDA source (.cu) files and compiled with nvcc, rather than being generated as Python-level (e.g., Triton / lazy-evaluated PyTorch) code, so that Python's lazy evaluation cannot be exploited to defer computation outside the timed region.

verification.spec: Inspect the kernel-generation pipeline output: assert all generated candidate kernels are emitted as .cu files (glob for .cu extension in output dir) and that the build step invokes nvcc on them. Additionally, feed a candidate written as Python/Triton — assert the pipeline rejects it or does not attempt to run it as an HGEMM candidate.

sub_tasks.requirements: The timing wrapper places a torch.cuda.synchronize() (or equivalent full device sync) both immediately before starting the timed region and immediately after ending it, so that all launched work is guaranteed materialized within the measured window.

verification.spec: Statically read the source of the kernel timing utility. Confirm that torch.cuda.synchronize() (or an equivalent full-device sync) appears BOTH immediately before start_event.record() AND immediately after end_event.record()/before elapsed_time is read, matching Listing 1 lines 1 and 7.

sub_tasks.requirements: The full benchmarking protocol is wired end-to-end into the reporting pipeline used for Table 1 / Figure 1.

Code has been implemented that, for each (M, N, K) configuration, runs the protocol (warmup, min-30s measurement, randomized order, offline or server mode) and produces a single per-configuration mean speedup value that is later aggregated across configurations for reporting.

verification.spec: Invoke the per-configuration evaluation function with a mock kernel over a small set of (M,N,K) values, e.g., {(128,128,128),(256,256,256)}, in both offline and server mode. Assert the returned object maps each (M,N,K) to exactly one scalar mean-speedup value per mode, and that the warmup-then-30s protocol was executed (via injected timer probe reporting elapsed measurement wall time >=30s).

sub_tasks.requirements: The same protocol is applied uniformly to every baseline (torch.matmul, cuBLAS-NN/TN, cuBLASLt-heuristic-NN/TN, cuBLASLt-AutoTuning-NN/TN) and to the CUDA-L2 kernel, so cross-baseline comparisons are apples-to-apples.
